title: GitHub: saving your work with a reverse gear
promise: You're going to have your project uploaded to github.com in a private repository, which is your project's folder saved there and visible only to you. You'll mark and name the version that works. And you'll deliberately break a file and recover it in under two minutes. All with the mouse, without typing a single command.
why: Ruben runs a hair salon in a Chicago suburb. He built a website with Claude so people could book their own appointments. It took him three afternoons to get the form sending the email with the reserved time correctly. On the fourth afternoon he asked the AI to change the button color. The AI rewrote the entire page file and the form stopped sending anything. There was no copy anywhere. So he lost the three afternoons and started over from zero. With what's in this lesson, that scare gets fixed in two clicks and fifteen seconds. Yesterday's work stays saved, whole, waiting for you to come back to it.

theory.title: A commit isn't a copy: it's a snapshot of the whole project
theory.text: When you save a file in your folder or in Drive, the new version overwrites the old one. GitHub works the other way around. Every time you upload changes, GitHub saves a complete snapshot of the project at that instant. The snapshot carries the date, your name, and a note you write explaining what you touched. That snapshot is called a commit. The previous snapshot doesn't get deleted or replaced: it stays whole in the history and you can open it whenever you want. Same with every one you make after. That's why you can point at any moment in the past and say "I want to go back to being like this," with nothing prepared beforehand. A reasonable doubt will come up: doesn't Drive work just as well, since it also saves versions? Drive saves versions file by file. Your project is forty files that only work together. Recovering yesterday's file A while leaving today's file B usually leaves you with a website more broken than before. GitHub saves all forty at once, at the same instant. That's why what you recover always fits together.
theory.analogy: Drive is a photocopier: the new copy replaces the old one and loose scraps of the old one are all that's left. GitHub is a camera with an infinite roll of film, and every shot captures the whole project with everyone in place. You never develop half a photo.
theory.example: A website project with 40 files and 300 KB of code barely takes up any space. With 200 commits stacked on top, on GitHub it weighs less than two phone photos. The history doesn't fill up and doesn't expire: it's text, and text weighs nothing.

theory.title: Account, repository, commit, branch: the whole map in four words
theory.text: The account is yours and is genuinely free: $0, no card at any step. With it you can create as many projects as you want. The repository (repo, for short) is a project's folder saved on github.com with its history inside. Make one per project, never one big one for everything. Each repository is public or private. Public means anyone on the planet can read it, even though only you can change it. Private means only you and whoever you invite can see it. Always start private: switching to public afterward is two clicks. Going the other way doesn't work the same, because what's already been seen has been seen and might be copied. The commit is each of those snapshots you keep saving. And the branch is a parallel copy of the project where you try things out without touching the good version. The main branch is called main and it's the one that counts. With these four words you understand ninety percent of what you'll see on screen.
theory.example: The username you pick shows up in the address of all your projects: github.com/marta-lopez/booking-site. Changing it later is possible, but it breaks every link you've already sent out. Choose something you could show a client without needing to explain.

theory.title: All of this is done by dragging files, not typing commands
theory.text: GitHub's bad reputation comes from the terminal and commands like git add, git commit, and git push. For what you need today, none of that is necessary. The "Add file" button and its "Upload files" option let you drag the project folder straight from your file explorer. GitHub keeps subfolders exactly as they are. There are three limits worth knowing before you drag anything. All three produce errors that look serious and aren't. One: through the browser you can't upload any single file over 25 MB. And no file in a repository can ever exceed 100 MB, no exceptions. Two: a hundred files per batch at most. If your project has more, upload it in two or three rounds. Three: empty folders don't upload, because to GitHub a folder with nothing in it doesn't exist. And if you ever need to touch several files in a row without downloading anything, open your repository and press the period key. A full editor opens right inside the browser, at github.dev, free and nothing to install.
theory.analogy: It's the same move as attaching photos to an email, but with whole folders and one difference: here the upload stays saved forever and numbered.
theory.example: The node_modules folder in a Next.js project usually has over 30,000 files and weighs 400 MB. It doesn't fit and doesn't need uploading, because it regenerates itself on any computer. Take it out of the selection before dragging and you avoid the error.

theory.title: The commit message is the label on the box
theory.text: Every time you upload something, GitHub asks for a note. It's a small text box and takes five seconds to fill in. It looks like a formality, but that's where whether your reverse gear will ever be useful gets decided. Three weeks from now the history won't show you the code: it'll show you a list of your notes. And you'll have to choose which day to go back to reading just that. "Update," "changes," and "asdf" are the same note written three ways, and all three leave you stranded. A useful note says where you touched and what you did, like "Booking form: add phone field and warn if empty." There's a very reliable tell hidden here. If you're struggling to write the note in one line, you've bundled five different changes into the same save. And the day you want to undo just one, you won't be able to. The practical rule is one commit per finished thing. And the message always starts with the area of the project you touched.
theory.example: A real 20-line history where seventeen say "Update" takes about twenty minutes to decipher, opening each change one by one. That same history with decent notes reads in fifteen seconds.

theory.title: The four reverse gears, from gentlest to bluntest
theory.text: The first is the one you'll use most: recovering a single file. Open it in GitHub, click "History," and pick the version from before the disaster. Copy its content and paste it over the current one. This fixes the typical case: the AI wrecked one page and the rest of the project is still fine. The second is going back to a marked version. If, on the day everything worked, you created a Release (a named version, like v1-working), its page has a "Source code (zip)" link that downloads the entire project as it stood that day. The third is the same, but for a random date you never marked: you go into that day's commit and download the zip from there. And the fourth: if the change came in as a pull request, its page has a "Revert" button that undoes it on its own, no copying or pasting needed. And now the warning almost nobody gives you, which will save you an afternoon of searching. GitHub's website has no undo button for a lone commit made directly on main. The "Revert" button only shows up on already-merged pull requests. That's why it's worth making changes you're nervous about on a separate branch, even if at first it seems like an unnecessary detour. That detour is exactly what turns your reverse gear into a button, instead of a copy-paste.
theory.analogy: It's like carrying four keys of different sizes: one opens a drawer, another a room, the big one the front door, and the fourth is the intercom button. It's maddening to discover, on the day you're in a rush, that you only had the small one on you.

theory.title: The one thing with no reverse gear: a key uploaded by mistake
theory.text: If your project talks to OpenAI, Anthropic, or Stripe, it uses an API key: a very long password that usually lives in a file called .env. That file never gets uploaded. And here's the trap that catches almost everyone: uploading it and deleting it afterward doesn't help. The history keeps every snapshot, so the key is still in there. It stays visible in the old commit, forever, one click away. If this happens to you, the only real fix is going to the website of whoever issued the key, revoking it, and generating a new one. Deleting the file on GitHub protects absolutely nothing. GitHub has an automatic detector that blocks uploads when it recognizes the format of some known keys. It saves a lot of people, but it doesn't know every format and doesn't scan what was already uploaded before. In public repositories there are programs scanning for keys around the clock. People have received bills for thousands of dollars within hours of a leak. The other serious thing in this world is deleting a whole repository. GitHub lets you try to recover it within the following 90 days from Settings, but that's an attempt, not a guarantee.
theory.example: An Anthropic key starts with sk-ant- and runs over a hundred characters. Imagine it shows up in a file you're about to upload. The right response isn't "I'll just remove it." It's "I'll revoke it at console.anthropic.com and generate a new one." Revoking and regenerating costs $0 and thirty seconds.

tasks.title: Create your GitHub account
tasks.action: Go to github.com and click "Sign up," top right. It'll ask you three things in a row, one screen each: email, a password, and a username. The password needs at least 15 characters, or 8 if you mix in a number and a lowercase letter. The username only allows letters, numbers, and hyphens: no spaces, no accented characters. That name shows up in the address of all your projects. Pick something short and presentable, like marta-lopez or vitoria-shop, not xXpepe1987Xx. Then it shows you a small puzzle to confirm you're a person. And it sends an eight-digit code to your email: type it in and you're in. It never asks for a card. The free plan costs $0 and includes unlimited projects, public and private.
tasks.expect: You land on a dashboard with a green button that says "Create repository" or "New." To confirm it worked, type github.com/YOUR-USERNAME into the browser bar: your profile should show up, empty but yours, with your name at the top.
tasks.stuck: If the code doesn't arrive in two minutes, check your spam folder for the sender noreply@github.com. If it still doesn't show up, go back to the GitHub tab and click "Resend code." If the username you want is already taken, GitHub tells you instantly in red below the box. Add your city or your trade instead of random numbers, since you won't remember the numbers later.

tasks.title: Turn on two-factor authentication and save your recovery codes
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, in Settings → Password and authentication
tasks.action: GitHub requires this from everyone who uploads code. It's better to do it now, calmly, than the day the warning pops up mid-task. Click your photo top right and choose "Settings." In the left column, click "Password and authentication." Inside, in the "Two-factor authentication" block, click "Enable two-factor authentication." The simplest option is the app-based one. Download Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator on your phone, both free. Scan the square on your computer screen with it and type the six digits it shows you. Right after, GitHub shows you a list of recovery codes. Download them with the "Download" button and save them wherever you keep important things, but outside your phone: they're precisely for the day you lose your phone.
tasks.expect: In "Password and authentication," the "Two-factor authentication" block shows a green check and the word "Enabled." And you have a text file on your computer with sixteen recovery codes in it.
tasks.stuck: If the phone app gives you a code and GitHub says it's invalid, it's almost always your phone's clock. Go into date and time settings, turn on automatic time, and try again. If the phone step stresses you out, GitHub also accepts receiving the code by SMS, though it's less secure. Turn that on today and switch to the app when you can.

tasks.title: Ask the AI which files you should NOT upload
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app, in the conversation where you have your project
tasks.action: Before dragging anything, you need to know what stays out. Some things don't fit, and some things should never be seen. Open the conversation where the AI built your project and paste the prompt below. It'll give you back two lists and a file called .gitignore, which is the list of things that never get uploaded. With the exclusion list in hand, open the project folder on your computer and check which of those names actually exist. Whichever are there, don't select them later when uploading.
tasks.prompt:
I'm about to upload my project folder to GitHub for the first time, dragging the files from the website. I don't use the terminal and don't want to.

My project is this: [DESCRIBE IT IN ONE LINE. FOR EXAMPLE: "an appointment booking site built with Next.js" or "a Python script that sorts PDF invoices"]

And here's what's inside the folder: [PASTE THE FILE AND FOLDER NAMES HERE. IF YOU DON'T KNOW HOW TO GET THE LIST, TAKE A SCREENSHOT OF THE OPEN FOLDER AND ATTACH IT INSTEAD OF TYPING IT]

Do four things for me, in this order and no fluff:

1) The list of what I SHOULD upload.

2) The list of what I should NOT upload and, next to each, in one sentence, why: too big, regenerates on its own, or contains passwords.

3) Tell me if my folder has any file that might contain API keys, passwords, or real customer personal data. If it does, put it first of all and warn me IN CAPITAL LETTERS, with the exact file name.

4) Write me the content of a .gitignore file for this specific project, ready to copy in full, with a short comment above each block of lines.

Don't explain what Git is or give me terminal commands. Direct, no fluff.
tasks.expect: Two clear lists and a text block for the .gitignore. If your project has them, the list of what NOT to upload should include: node_modules, .env, .env.local, the .next or dist or build folder, the .venv folder, and any file ending in .key or .pem.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you terminal commands, reply: "I'm not going to use the terminal, I upload by dragging from github.com; just give me the two lists and the .gitignore content." If you don't know how to get the file list, open the folder in your explorer and take a screenshot. Paste it into the chat: ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini read images without a problem.

tasks.title: Create the repository, private and with a README
tasks.action: Click the + sign top right, to the left of your photo, and choose "New repository." You can also go directly to github.com/new. Fill in four things. In "Repository name," the project name with no spaces or accents: booking-site, not "Booking Site." In "Description," one line saying what it is. Check "Private," always, even if the project has nothing secret in it. And below, check the "Add a README file" box, which creates the project's presentation file. If the AI told you the tech stack in the previous task, open the "Add .gitignore" dropdown and look for the matching template (Node, Python, etc.). Finish with the green "Create repository" button.
tasks.expect: Your repository's page, with the address github.com/your-username/booking-site in the browser bar. You'll see the README.md file listed and, below it, its content with the project name as a big heading. Above, next to the repository name, a gray tag that says "Private."
tasks.stuck: Is the green button grayed out and unclickable? The name has a disallowed character, or you already used it on another project of yours. Remove accents, spaces, and symbols. If you can't find the + sign, it's in the top right corner, right to the left of your profile photo. You need to click the small arrow next to it.

tasks.title: Upload the project by dragging the folder
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, inside the repository you just created
tasks.action: Click the "Add file" button, next to the green "Code" button, and choose "Upload files." A large area opens with a dotted box. Open the project folder on your computer in another window. Select everything except what the AI told you to leave out, and drag it into the box. You can drag whole folders: GitHub keeps the subfolder structure as-is. Wait for all the names to show up listed below; with thirty files it takes a few seconds. Scroll down, there are two text boxes. In the first, write "First upload of the complete project." Leave "Commit directly to the main branch" checked and click the green "Commit changes" button.
tasks.expect: You're back on the repository's front page and see your folders and files listed, with "now" or "a few seconds ago" next to them. Top right of that list, next to a clock icon, it says "2 Commits." Click any file: your code should show up inside.
tasks.stuck: If you get the message "Yowza, that's a big file," you've included a file over 25 MB: remove it from the selection and upload the rest without it. If you drag and nothing happens, click the blue "choose your files" link and select them manually. If your project has more than a hundred files, upload the main folders first and the rest in a second batch. Each batch will be one more commit, and that doesn't break anything.

tasks.title: Make a change from the website and write a message that's actually useful
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, inside your repository
tasks.action: Click the README.md file to open it on its own. Click the pencil icon top right; hovering says "Edit this file." Write three lines inside: what the project does, what address it'll be seen at once published, and today's date. Click the green "Commit changes..." button. A small window opens asking for the message, and this is where it's decided whether it'll be worth anything. Use the prompt below if it doesn't come naturally. Paste the message, leave "Commit directly to the main branch" checked, and confirm. Then go back to the front page and click where it shows the commit count, next to the clock icon.
tasks.prompt:
I'm about to save a change on GitHub and need to write the commit message, the short note explaining what I changed. Three weeks from now that note will be the only thing I see to decide which version to go back to, so it has to be useful.

What I touched is this: [DESCRIBE IT IN YOUR OWN WORDS, NO ORDER NEEDED AND DON'T WORRY ABOUT REPEATING YOURSELF. EVERYTHING YOU REMEMBER CHANGING]

Write me the message following these exact rules:
- A single line, maximum 70 characters.
- Start with the area of the project I touched, a colon, then what I did. Example: "Contact form: add required phone field."
- Present tense.
- Banned words: "update," "various changes," "improvements," and "fixes."

One more thing: if from what I told you, you see that I've bundled two or more unrelated changes together, tell me clearly and suggest how to split it into two separate saves, with a message for each.

Give me only the message or messages. No explanation, no alternatives, no questions.
tasks.expect: In the history list you now see two or three lines. Each carries your message, your username, the date, and to the right a short seven-character code of letters and numbers. Click one: the change screen opens, with removed lines in red and added ones in green.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the pencil, you're looking at the file from the repository's front page. Click the file name first to open it on its own. If the green button says "Propose changes" instead of "Commit changes," you're on a branch that isn't main. Go back to the front page and check that the dropdown top left says "main."

tasks.title: Mark the working version with a name
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, in the right column of your repository's front page
tasks.action: On the repository's front page, scroll down the right column until you find "Releases," below the "About" block. Click "Create a new release." At the top click the "Choose a tag" dropdown, type v1-working, and pick the option that shows below: "+ Create new tag: v1-working on publish." In "Release title" put something like "Working version - August 19." In the big description box write two lines about what already works, with real detail: "The site loads on mobile and desktop. The booking form sends the email with the chosen time." At the bottom, green "Publish release" button.
tasks.expect: A new page with your version's title and, at the bottom, two links GitHub generates automatically: "Source code (zip)" and "Source code (tar.gz)." That zip is your entire project frozen at this moment. Back on the front page, in the right column, Releases now says "v1-working" with the "Latest" tag.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the Releases section, scroll further: it's below the "About" block and on narrow screens it goes all the way to the bottom. If the tag dropdown won't let you type, click inside the search box that appears when you open it and type there. If it asks for a "Target," leave it on main.

tasks.title: Break a file on purpose and recover it
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, inside your repository
tasks.action: This is a drill and it needs to happen today, calmly, not the day of the actual scare. Open any file that isn't the README, click the pencil, and delete half a screen of content. Save with the message "Drill: breaking this file on purpose." Now recover it. With the file open, click the "History" button, top right of the code box. Up comes the list of every commit that touched that specific file. Click the one from before the wreck. On that screen, to the right of the file name, there's a three-dot button: open it and choose "View file." There's the whole file exactly as it was. Click the copy icon, top right of the code. Go back to your current file and click the pencil. Select everything with Ctrl+A (Cmd+A on Mac), paste over it, and save with the message "Restore file to the version before the drill."
tasks.prompt:
I'm going to paste two versions of the same project file. The first is the one that worked, pulled from GitHub's history. The second is what I have right now, broken.

WORKING VERSION:
[PASTE THE FULL CONTENT OF THE FILE FROM THE HISTORY HERE]

CURRENT VERSION, BROKEN:
[PASTE THE FULL CONTENT OF THE FILE AS IT IS NOW]

Answer me three things, briefly:

1) What changed from one to the other, as a list of plain-English sentences. Don't paste code at this point.

2) Which of those changes is the one that breaks the site and why.

3) If the broken version has something good worth keeping, tell me and then give me the complete final file, merging the good parts of both, ready to select and paste in one go over the current one.

Don't give me terminal commands or explain how Git works. If the final file is long, give it to me whole anyway: I'm going to paste it all at once, not in pieces.
tasks.expect: The file has the old content back. And in its history you now have three entries in a row: the good one, the broken one, and the restored one. Notice something important: the wreck's commit is still there, never deleted. That's how this works: the history never gets trimmed, only new snapshots get added on top.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find "History," look at the top line of the code box, where the line count and file size show. On narrow screens it hides behind the three-dot icon. If pasting leaves the file with duplicated content, you didn't select everything before pasting: undo with Ctrl+Z and try again.

tasks.title: Recover the whole project from a specific date
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, in the commit history
tasks.action: This is the big reverse gear, the one for the day the AI rewrites six files and you don't even know which ones. On the repository's front page, click the commit count, next to the clock icon. Look through the list for the last point where everything was fine; the message you wrote at the time is what'll tell you. To the right of that line there's a button with the "<>" symbol that, on hover, says "Browse the repository at this point in the history." Click it: you're now looking at your project exactly as it stood that day. Click the green "Code" button and choose "Download ZIP." Unzip it into a new folder on your computer. Open it and check with your own eyes that what you were looking for is there, before touching anything else.
tasks.expect: A .zip file in your Downloads folder with the repository's name and the commit's short code in the file name, like booking-site-a1b2c3d.zip. Once unzipped, the files are exactly as they stood that day, not as they stand today.
tasks.stuck: If the "Code" button doesn't offer "Download ZIP," check that you're on the "Code" tab of the repository and not inside a single file. If node_modules is missing after unzipping, that's normal and not a problem: it never gets uploaded and regenerates on its own. And watch out for one trap when re-uploading that old zip by dragging it in. GitHub overwrites the files that match, but doesn't delete files that exist today and didn't exist back then. You have to delete those yourself from the website: open each one, click the three-dot button, then "Delete file."

tasks.title: Set up a real undo button: branch, pull request, and Revert
tasks.where: On the GitHub website, inside your repository
tasks.action: From today on, changes you're nervous about get made this way. Open a file, click the pencil, and change something. When clicking "Commit changes...", in the small window choose the second option, the one below: "Create a new branch for this commit and start a pull request." It suggests a branch name like your-username-patch-1. Delete it and write something meaningful instead, like test-button-color. Click "Propose changes." GitHub takes you to a screen to open the pull request: give it a title and click "Create pull request." Before accepting anything, go into the "Files changed" tab, which shows in green and red exactly what changes, line by line. Give it to the AI with the prompt below. If it convinces you, go back to the "Conversation" tab, click "Merge pull request," then "Confirm merge." And now the payoff: on that same page, right below the merge message, a gray button appears that says "Revert."
tasks.prompt:
I'm about to accept a change in my project and want a second opinion before merging it into the good version. I'm pasting what changes exactly as GitHub shows it to me: lines starting with a minus sign are removed and lines starting with a plus sign are added.

[PASTE WHAT YOU SEE IN THE "FILES CHANGED" TAB HERE. IF IT'S VERY LONG, PASTE ONLY THE FILES YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND]

Answer me like this, in this order:

1) In two plain-English sentences: what this change does.

2) Could it break something that currently works? If you think so, tell me exactly which screen or which button on my site I should open and test before accepting it.

3) Is there any password, API key, real email, or real phone number in here that shouldn't stay saved forever? If there is, put it first and IN CAPITAL LETTERS.

4) A one-line verdict: ACCEPT or DON'T ACCEPT, and why.

Don't give me terminal commands and don't explain how Git works.
tasks.expect: After merging, the change is now in main. And in the "Pull requests" tab, under "Closed," your request shows up in purple with the word "Merged." If you click "Revert," GitHub creates another pull request with the change reversed. Once accepted, the project goes back to how it was and the history keeps both, the going and the coming back.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the "Revert" button, check the request is actually merged (purple, "Merged") and not just closed (red, "Closed"): the button only shows on merged ones. If merging warns you about conflicts, it means the same chunk of a file got touched from two different places. At your level, the fastest fix is closing that request without merging, deleting the branch with the "Delete branch" button, and redoing the change directly on main.

matters: Writing a commit message that says where you touched and what you did. It's the only clue you'll have on the day of the scare. With twenty lines that all say "Update," you have to open each change one by one until you find the right one. That's twenty minutes of anxiety hunting for something you should find in fifteen seconds.

Never uploading the .env file or any API key. Uploading it and deleting it afterward does nothing, because the history keeps every snapshot and the key stays visible in the old one forever. The only real way out is revoking that key on the website of whoever issued it and generating a new one. And if it was a paid key, the bill can arrive before the warning does.

Uploading changes often, not once a month. You can only go back to the points you've saved. So if you save every three weeks, your reverse gear is three weeks of lost work. The habit that works is uploading every time something starts working, even something small. And always before asking the AI for a big change.

Marking the working version as a Release, with a name and a date. With sixty unmarked commits, finding "the last one that worked" is half an afternoon of trial and error. With a Release called v1-working it's one click and a zip. It takes ninety seconds to do, and you only appreciate it once you've already done it.
ignore: The terminal and Git commands: git add, git commit, git push, git pull. Everything in this lesson is done with the mouse from github.com. For a project you're running solo, the website serves you for months. The terminal brings speed once you're already uploading changes ten times a day, not before.

Complicated branches, rebases, merge conflicts, and named workflows. Main plus one test branch when something makes you nervous is all you need. That covers ninety-five percent of what you'll do this year.

GitHub Actions, which runs automated tasks every time you upload something. And Codespaces, which gives you a coding computer inside your browser. Both are included in the free plan and will still be there the day you need them. Right now they solve problems you don't have yet.
canDo: Write the exact content of the .gitignore file for your specific project, if you tell it what tech it uses. And warn you which of your files smell like a password before you upload them.

Turn your messy explanation of what you touched into a one-line commit message that makes sense three weeks from now. And tell you if what you did is actually two separate changes that should be split.
Read an entire public repository by its address and explain what each file does and where to start looking. Private ones need explicit permission granted through the app's connectors.
Compare two versions of a file you paste in. It tells you which specific line changed and which one breaks the site. And it merges the good parts of both into a final file.
cantDo: It can't click github.com's buttons for you from the text box. Creating the account, dragging the folder, and confirming the commit are things you do yourself with the mouse. The AI accompanies you, it doesn't replace you.

It doesn't find out you've broken something. Nobody's going to warn you that the form stopped sending emails three days ago. That warning is on you, opening the site and testing it after every change.

It can't recover what you never uploaded. If the good change only lived on your computer and the AI overwrote it, GitHub doesn't have it and there's nothing to rescue. That's why you upload before asking for the change, not after.

It can't delete a key from your repository's history or make it stop being published. Removing the line from the file today doesn't remove it from yesterday's snapshot, and no AI can rewrite those snapshots from the website.
words: Repository
A project's folder saved on GitHub's website, with its whole past inside. It opens at an address like github.com/your-name/your-project. One per project.
Commit
Each save. It's a snapshot of the entire project at a specific moment, with the date, who made it, and a note explaining what was touched. Previous snapshots never get deleted.
Commit message
The short note you write when saving. Three weeks from now it'll be the only thing you read to decide which day to go back to. That's why it needs to say where you touched and what you did.
Branch
A parallel copy of the project for trying things out without touching the good version. If it goes wrong, you throw away the copy and nothing happened. The good, main copy is called main.
Pull request
A formal notice inside GitHub that says: I've changed this in a separate copy, look at what changes and decide whether it goes into the good one.
Merge
Accepting those changes and folding them into the good version. The button says "Merge," and once clicked, GitHub offers you the button to undo the whole thing right next to it.
Revert

Undoing an already-accepted change. GitHub doesn't delete anything: it adds a new save that puts things back the way they were. The button says "Revert" and only shows up on already-merged pull requests.
README

The presentation file you see when entering your project, written in plain text. It explains what this is, what it's for, and how to get it running. It's the first thing anyone reads, including you six months from now.
.gitignore
A list of file and folder names that never get uploaded, not even by accident. Passwords go there, along with anything that takes up a lot of space and can regenerate itself.
Release
A named, dated version, marked by hand on the day everything works. Like v1-working. It lets you go back there with one click without digging through the save list.
